title: PACE: Unleashing the Power of Code Embeddings to Boost AutoML Agents

problem.claim: LLM-driven AutoML agents construct end-to-end machine learning pipelines, but costly execution-based feedback makes high-quality solution search inefficient under restricted computational budgets.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies a need for pre-execution candidate utility estimation that does not require training a separate offline predictor.

contributions.claim: PACE is an online-adaptive admission control framework that estimates candidate utility before execution from within-run execution history.
PACE uses multi-view semantic embeddings, dynamic clustering of executed candidates, proximity to historical elite regions, and adaptive view reweighting to estimate candidate potential.
PACE functions as a plug-and-play admission layer for AutoML agents, either as an execution gate or as a search prior.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In the tested settings, PACE improves the density of elite solutions found within fixed computational budgets.
PACE achieves this reported improvement without modifying the underlying agent architecture.
The authors report that code, configurations, and prompt templates are publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM-driven AutoML agents can construct end-to-end machine learning pipelines.
Execution-based feedback is costly and makes search inefficient under restricted budgets.
PACE estimates candidate utility before execution using within-run history, embeddings, clustering, elite-region proximity, and adaptive view weighting.
The admission signal biases search toward promising regions while retaining exploration when local structure is weak.
PACE operates as a plug-and-play gate or search prior and reportedly increases elite-solution density within fixed budgets without changing agent architecture.

source_observation.claim: Within-run execution history can be used to estimate candidate utility before incurring execution cost.

interpretation.claim: A search system may improve budget efficiency by using online structural signals instead of relying only on post-execution evaluation.

application.claim: For budget-constrained automated search, consider an adaptive admission layer based on semantic similarity to historically strong candidates.

exception.claim: The abstract indicates that exploration should be retained when local structure is weak, so admission should not always favor exploitation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, benchmarks, baselines, or quantitative improvement magnitudes.
The abstract does not describe the tested computational budgets or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not report limitations or failure cases beyond the stated need to retain exploration when local structure is weak.
